reasoning.notes: Players often tracked which cards remained in hands they had seen, counted the maki and squid still in play, and denied specific cards to a wasabi-holding or set-completing left neighbour. Some picks are only 'sure X points' comparisons, and a few inferences were off, but most decisions rest on specific, mostly correct reads of the state.

evidence.quote: The only other maki card still in play is one Maki-1, so seat 3 (now on 6) can reach at most 7. That locks in first place in maki.
evidence.shows: Counts the maki left in play to work out the rival's ceiling.

evidence.quote: Tracking the passed hands shows the last card I receive must be a Tempura... seats 4 and 1 can only take two of them first.
evidence.shows: Reconstructs the hidden hands to prove which card will arrive last.

evidence.quote: The Dumpling I pass on cannot raise seat 3's maki, because the cards it now holds came from me and are only Dumpling and Tempura.
evidence.shows: Reasons from remembered contents about what the left neighbour can still reach.

evidence.quote: Seat 2 has 2 sashimi, so a passed Sashimi would complete their set for 10 points. A passed Tempura is worth at most 5 to them.
evidence.shows: Weighs what each card is worth to the left neighbour, the denial the designer describes.

evidence.quote: I get 3 points either way, as a tie for first or as second place. So the maki card would add nothing for me.
evidence.shows: Predicts the rival's maki pickups and sees that a maki card has no marginal value.

planning.notes: Players set up wasabi for a nigiri they expect to come back, built sets across picks from cards they had seen, and managed the pudding race across hands. Several multi-pick plans that depended on opponents' predicted choices were made and carried out.

evidence.quote: Seat 4 picks from that hand first, but they have 1 tempura, so they will most likely take Tempura to complete a pair worth 5. That would make the salmon worth 6 to me
evidence.shows: A two-pick plan that relies on the neighbour's choice; seat 4 did take Tempura and seat 1 put the Salmon on wasabi at turn 72.

evidence.quote: If I take Maki-1 now and another Maki-1 next pick, I reach 9. Seat 4 can reach at most 8, so I win the 6 maki points outright
evidence.shows: A two-pick maki plan, carried out at turn 74.

evidence.quote: The hand I passed at pick 2 still holds 2 Sashimi and comes back to me at pick 6, so a third Sashimi for the 10-point set is reasonably likely.
evidence.shows: Builds a set on cards expected to return; the set was completed at turn 13.

evidence.quote: If I take this pudding, I avoid that penalty, and seat 4 would be alone at fewest and take the full -6.
evidence.shows: Uses the cross-hand pudding race against the leader.

luck.notes: Final margins were small (3-8 points), and which cards were dealt into which hands, plus last-card gambles, swung several hand scores. Choices still clearly shaped the results, through maki wins, denial and pudding.

evidence.quote: a third Tempura only pays if my last card is also a Tempura (+5)
evidence.shows: A late gamble on the last card's identity; the last card was Sashimi.

evidence.quote: if my last card is a Sashimi I complete a set for 10 points
evidence.shows: A 10-point outcome riding on which card is left over.

weak_spots.what: Claimed taking the Salmon 'keeps it from seat 1, who has an unused Wasabi', but seat 3 passes to seat 4, so seat 1 was not next to receive it. The denial reasoning misread the passing order.

Dismissed Pudding as 'worth only a point or two over the whole game' while on 0 puddings, with the others on 1 and 2. Later picks had to chase puddings, and seat 3 still finished tied for fewest. The pudding swing was undervalued.

Took Wasabi, betting the last card might be a nigiri, after concluding at turn 50 that the last card 'must be a Tempura'. Neither card could score here, but the reasoning contradicted the player's own correct deduction.

summary: Winning requires real reasoning and planning: tracking cards in rotating hands, denying the left neighbour, timing wasabi and nigiri, and the cross-hand pudding race all showed up and decided close games. Making the deal less lopsided, or rewarding long cross-hand commitments more, would lower the share of results decided by which cards happen to land in which hand.
